metadata.title: Burgerschap in het voortgezet onderwijs: Nederland in vergelijkend perspectief

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study reports ICCS 2016 data collection in the Netherlands among students in the second year of secondary education, with a school and class sampling procedure following ICCS prescriptions. The analytic sample is described as 2812 students from 123 participating schools (one class per school), with one school excluded due to low student response. The manuscript does not report the use of ICCS sampling weights or any replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the presented analyses. Because the book primarily reports descriptive and regression-based results rather than ML model training, and because no weight variable names or complex-survey procedures are documented, weighting cannot be confirmed from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This report does not present an ML pipeline on PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes; instead it describes ICCS citizenship knowledge/attitudes/skills and school practices using IRT/Rasch-scaled scores and regression models. Plausible values (PV) handling is therefore not applicable to the reported outcomes as framed in the manuscript (the knowledge scale is described as Rasch/IRT-scaled rather than PV-based). The manuscript also does not document a specific missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation) for the reported analyses, representing a reporting gap for missingness handling.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used ICCS 2016 Netherlands main study data collected in Feb–Apr 2016 among students in the second year of secondary education. Sampling followed ICCS rules: 124 schools were initially selected, but one school was excluded because less than 50% of students participated in the selected class; final student data cover 123 schools and 2812 students. One class per participating school was selected; participating schools were randomly selected according to strict ICCS sampling prescriptions. The manuscript also notes non-response among selected students (e.g., absence, no parental consent, not enrolled anymore), but does not specify an explicit missing-data imputation/deletion rule for the analytic models.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 Netherlands (secondary school, Grade 8/second year) — Citizenship knowledge and attitudes
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported as ML metrics (regression coefficients reported in tables; e.g., Model 2/3 coefficients for learning and class climate).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 Netherlands the study leveraged socioeconomic background, language spoken at home, expected higher education, and school-level citizenship learning and discussion climate to explain citizenship knowledge, finding that learning about citizenship at school and participation in citizenship activities are positively related to citizenship knowledge (with some effects differing by country and becoming non-significant after adding background characteristics). This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 Netherlands (secondary school, Grade 8/second year) — Citizenship attitudes and engagement
main_findings.target_variable: Verwacht toekomstig stemgedrag (expected future voting behavior)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported as ML metrics (multiple regression coefficients reported; e.g., Table 4.4.3 and 4.4.4 show unstandardized coefficients with standard errors).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 Netherlands the study leveraged gender, socioeconomic background, interest in political issues, and participation in citizenship activities to model expected future voting behavior, finding that citizenship skills/knowledge and conventional citizenship attitudes (e.g., importance of voting) and trust in institutions are positively associated with expected future voting, while participation effects vary by country. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: This ICCS 2016 Netherlands report describes citizenship knowledge, attitudes, skills, and related behaviors among 2812 students in the second year of secondary education from 123 participating schools, and compares results with 23 other countries. The manuscript does not train machine-learning models; instead it reports descriptive statistics and regression-based associations using IRT/Rasch-scaled outcomes and questionnaire/school-context measures. Key results include that Dutch students’ citizenship knowledge is around the international average but below that of similar countries, and that school-level citizenship learning and an open class climate for discussion are associated with higher citizenship knowledge (with some effects attenuating after controlling for background characteristics). For expected future voting behavior, citizenship skills/knowledge, conventional citizenship attitudes, and trust in institutions show positive associations, while participation effects differ across countries. The text does not document a missing-data strategy and does not specify PV handling, which limits transparency for any potential PV-based modeling assumptions.
